items.x: For anyone who wants to understand, deploy or integrate AI Workforce OS: how it is built, what the API exposes, how accounts are isolated and what can be configured. Everything describes what the code does today.

AI Workforce OS separates deciding from doing: a Go backend is the source of truth, a Python runtime only reasons with the model, and a Next.js frontend draws the office from events. This page is for anyone who deploys, extends or audits the system: how the pieces fit and how a request travels end to end.

All business state lives in the backend; the runtime keeps no state between calls. Postgres, Redis, object storage and the sandbox are optional in development and each has a fallback. Frontend · Next.js, React Three Fiber · 3D office and dashboard mode. Consumes REST and the WebSocket; every animation derives from real events. Backend · Go, chi · REST API /api/v1, WebSocket /ws, orchestrator, approvals, audit, budget, authentication and RBAC. Agent runtime · Python, FastAPI, CrewAI · Receives a task and context, calls the model provider and returns a structured result. Postgres · PostgreSQL · Data for all organizations, with row-level security and numbered SQL migrations. Without DATABASE_UR

The core rule: the runtime never talks to Postgres, Redis or external systems. It receives a task with its context and returns a result, tool requests and usage; it only contacts the model provider. The backend decides permissions, autonomy and budget, and is the only one that executes tools. The backend calls the runtime over HTTP with JSON at RUNTIME_URL. If RUNTIME_TOKEN is set on both sides, every call carries that secret as a bearer token. The AI engine sits behind an interface of its own (AgentEngine), so CrewAI can be replaced without touching the backend. The agent runtime has its own page with the full contract, the providers and the data policy. POST /v1/plan, /v1/plan-phases, /v1/

The user's ask reaches the orchestrator, which asks the runtime for a plan, validates it and creates tasks. Each task is run by an agent that may request tools; sensitive actions wait for human approval, and a report is synthesized at the end. The user submits text with POST /api/v1/requests (or through chat, which routes it). The backend answers 202 with request_id and emits request.received. The orchestrator asks the runtime for a plan and validates it before accepting it: duplicate keys, unknown or circular dependencies and maximum depth. It then emits plan.created and task.created. Tasks run respecting depends_on. Each one changes the agent state (agent.state_changed) and may trigger age

GET /ws opens one WebSocket per organization. The backend publishes each event to Redis (channel aiworkforce:events) and a hub forwards the frame only to clients whose org_id matches; a frame without org_id is dropped. A frame with an audience reaches only those users. On connect a hello event carries the agent list, followed by domain events. There is no replay, so the client must reload state over REST after reconnecting. The server pings every 30 s and closes if no pong arrives within 60 s. A slow client, with 256 frames queued, is disconnected. The org_id travels inside the access token and is never taken from client input. The HTTP layer puts it in the request context and every query is filtered by it. A user can belong to several organizations and switches between them by opening a new session. As defense in depth, Postgres enforces row-level security: Each transaction sets app.org_id with set_config(..., true), local to the transaction; the policies compare org_id with app_current_org(). If the value is missing, queries see and write no rows: they fail closed. The runtime's HTTP contract is the same in both modes; the engine changes. In simulation (with SIMULATION=true or with no provider configured) the runtime returns scripted results with simulated latencies, with no network and no cost. In live mode it uses the configured providers and its GET /healthz reports mode: live and the provider. If a provider is configured but the live engine cannot start, the runtime answers in simulation with status: degraded and a warning; there is no silent fallback. The backend reflects the mode in its own GET /healthz as runtime_mode. SIMULATION=true always wins: no network calls are made even when keys are present.

There are three Compose files: docker-compose.yml: development with accounts. Starts postgres, redis, objects (S3 storage), agent-runtime, backend and frontend; the sandbox runner is in the sandbox profile. docker-compose.demo.yml: layered on the previous one for the open demo mode (AUTH_ENABLED=false). docker-compose.prod.yml: production. caddy, postgres, redis, agent-runtime, backend and frontend; only Caddy publishes ports (80 and 443). In production Caddy terminates TLS, adds security headers (HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy) and routes by path: /api/* and /ws to the backend, everything else to the frontend.
The backend is layered: api depends on application, which depends on domain; infrastructure implements the ports.

The agent runtime is a Python service (FastAPI and CrewAI) that turns a task and its context into a structured result; it talks only to model providers. This page is for whoever runs or integrates the runtime: its HTTP contract, how it picks a provider, what data leaves the process and how cost is controlled.

The backend calls the runtime over HTTP with a task, the agent profile and the context it assembled. The runtime returns validated structured output and, if the agent wants to act, a list of tool_requests. It never executes a tool and never calls an external system: the model may be misled by untrusted text, but it can only propose. When RUNTIME_TOKEN is set, the runtime requires Authorization: Bearer <token> on every route except GET /healthz, compared in constant time; without it, it answers 401. The endpoints are: Set RUNTIME_TOKEN to the same value in the backend and the runtime. Without it, anyone who can reach the runtime port can spend your provider keys; the backend logs a warning at

The HTTP contract is the same in both modes; only the engine changes. Simulation: on with SIMULATION=true or when no provider is configured. It returns plausible plans, results, tokens and costs with simulated latency (SIM_LATENCY_SCALE=0 removes the delay), with no network and no cost, and it ignores the provider policy because no data leaves the process. Live: the CrewAI engine calls the provider and validates the output against the StructuredOutput schema. LLM_DIRECT_CALL=true replaces the CrewAI loop with a single chat call. Degraded: if a provider is configured but the live engine cannot start, the runtime answers in simulation and GET /healthz returns status: degraded with a warning. T

There are five providers. One counts as configured when its key is in the environment (for custom, the base URL is enough) or when the request carries the organization's own key. A custom model is passed as openai/<name>, and a free local model can be priced at 0 with CUSTOM_PRICE_IN_PER_M and CUSTOM_PRICE_OUT_PER_M. Organizations can bring their own key. It is sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key wrapped by CONNECTIONS_KEK, no API response returns it beyond its last four characters (key_last4), and it travels in clear only on the internal hop from the backend to the runtime. deepseek · DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, DEEPSEEK_MODEL · deepseek/deepseek-chat anthropic · ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_MODEL ·

For each call the runtime builds an attempt list. Each source adds only the providers not listed yet, so every configured and permitted provider ends up as a fallback: MODEL_PROVIDER_ORDER_<ROLE>: the agent role in capitals (for example MODEL_PROVIDER_ORDER_LEGAL) or the call kind: PLAN, REVIEW, CONSULT, SYNTHESIZE, SUMMARIZE, ROUTE, COUNTERARGUMENT. role_providers from the organization's model policy. The request's preferred_providers. The global MODEL_PROVIDER_ORDER (default deepseek,anthropic,openai,kimi,custom). A transient failure (timeout, rate limit, 5xx) is retried on the same provider PROVIDER_RETRIES times (default 1, waiting PROVIDER_RETRY_BACKOFF_S) before moving to the next; PRO

The data policy is applied before anything is sent. The effective list is the operator's ALLOWED_PROVIDERS intersected with the request's allowed_providers: a provider outside the list is neither called nor used as a fallback, and a request can narrow the operator ceiling but never widen it. The backend fills allowed_providers from each organization's model policy (GET/PUT /api/v1/settings/model-policy, owner and admin only, every change audited). When no provider is left it sends the sentinel value none, so the runtime refuses the call instead of widening the set. With byo_only, only the organization's own keys may answer. Failures are explicit: no_allowed_provider · 422 · No configured pro

A prompt may contain: The user's request text and the agent's persona, responsibilities and tools. Outputs of dependency tasks, agent memory and external content. Tool results that the backend already filtered and redacted. Consult or synthesis questions. Secrets are redacted twice. The backend redacts tool results first; the runtime's redact.py module is the second barrier and covers private keys, JWTs, GitHub, AWS and Google tokens, API keys, bearer tokens, password-style assignments, URLs carrying tokens and Luhn-valid card numbers. items.h: Tools: the model asks, the backend executes
items.x: A tool request is a proposal. The backend checks the agent's tool list, the arguments, the policy engine and the autonomy level, and may create an approval for a person. Only then does it run the tool, with credentials from the encrypted vault that never leave the backend. The result goes back to the model redacted and delimited as untrusted data. Capabilities that the provider manifest marks as irreversible, such as Gmail's email.send, always require a human decision, whatever the agent's autonomy. An approved action is claimed at most once, so a restart cannot run it twice. Tools without a real connection use in-memory fake adapters, which is how simulation works end to end.

The code.run action lets an agent ask to execute Python. It is available only when the backend has SANDBOX_URL and SANDBOX_TOKEN; without them it is denied with sandbox_unavailable. By default every run is an approval that shows the code, the input files and the purpose, and it is bound to the code hash and the SHA-256 of every input: changing either requires a new approval. After approval the backend sends the run to a separate runner that starts a disposable container: No network (--network none), a read-only root, a non-root user and all capabilities dropped. Time, memory, process and output-size limits (SANDBOX_MAX_RUNTIME_SECONDS, SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB, SANDBOX_PIDS, SANDBOX_MAX_OUTPUT_BYTE

Prices live in one table, model_prices.json, in USD per million tokens, byte-identical in the backend and the runtime (a test in each service enforces it). A model missing from the table is billed at the table's default rate and logged once. PRICE_IN_PER_M and PRICE_OUT_PER_M force a rate for every model. Before each call the backend reserves the maximum estimate against the request, the agent and the organization. Afterwards it records the greater of the runtime's reported cost and its own recalculation, so it does not depend on the runtime's accuracy. Spending is read from a ledger in Postgres and survives restarts. The price table is a budgeting reference, not what your own provider contr

The Go backend exposes a REST API under /api/v1 and an event channel at /ws. This reference is for anyone integrating or automating: it covers authentication, error conventions and the main routes as registered in the router, with examples you can copy.

All REST routes hang under /api/v1; the version is part of the path. The WebSocket (/ws) and the root health check (/healthz) live outside that prefix. Bodies are UTF-8 JSON, except drive uploads, which send the file as the raw body. Examples use localhost:8080; substitute your host. Every route on this page is relative to /api/v1 unless stated otherwise. With AUTH_ENABLED=false (demo mode) the API requires no authentication and everything runs on one fixed organization. Do not expose that mode to a network.

With AUTH_ENABLED=true, every route requires a token except /healthz, the public /auth/* routes, the OAuth callback and a few links that carry their own secret (signed approval links and the calendar feed). Login returns an access token (a JWT, 15 minutes) sent in the Authorization: Bearer header. The refresh token never appears in the JSON body: it travels in the HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie wfai_refresh, scoped to the /api/v1/auth path. Refresh and logout act on that cookie, so they also require the X-WFAI-CSRF header. The organization comes from the token, never from a parameter. For server-to-server integrations there is a separate API at /api/public/v1, authenticated with scoped API tokens instead of user sessions. The organization comes from the token. It needs Postgres; without it these routes are not mounted. An admin creates, lists and revokes tokens with POST/GET /governance/tokens and DELETE /governance/tokens/{id}. Creation body: name, scopes, expires_in_days. Each token allows 120 requests per minute; beyond that it answers 429 with Retry-After. GET /agents: scope agents:read. GET /conversations accepts limit and offset and returns X-Has-More and X-Next-Offset. GET /rewards/ledger accepts limit (default 50, maximum 200) and before; GET /agents/{id}/memory accepts limit and q. A project is a multi-node plan with a budget. The cycle is create a draft, edit the plan, estimate and validate, then launch with an approved budget. Pausing, cancelling and changing the budget of a running project are admin actions. Skills are reusable, versioned instructions. GET /ws opens your organization's event channel. On connect you receive hello with the agent list, then every domain event; an event with an audience reaches only the users it names. There are no topic subscriptions and no replay: after reconnecting, reload state over REST. The server pings every 30 s and closes if no pong arrives within 60 s. From the client it only processes small presence frames (position, status) when that feature is on; everything else is ignored. This page describes the auth service in the Go backend: accounts, sessions, two-factor authentication, roles, invitations and how Postgres enforces the boundary between organizations. It is for whoever deploys or operates AI Workforce OS or builds their own client against the API.

items.h: Two modes: AUTH_ENABLED false and true
items.x: With AUTH_ENABLED=false (the binary's default) there is no login: the API is open, every request uses a single fixed demo organization and the server logs a warning at startup. It is meant for local development and demos. With AUTH_ENABLED=true the API requires a bearer access token on protected routes, resolves the role on every request and scopes all data access to the caller's organization. Startup fails if: JWT_SECRET is shorter than 32 bytes. DATABASE_URL is missing (accounts and organizations live in Postgres). ALLOWED_ORIGINS contains *. If you leave it empty, only the same origin is accepted. The development docker-compose.yml starts with AUTH_ENABLED=true and AUTH_COOKIE_SECURE=fals

POST /api/v1/auth/register creates a user, a new organization and an owner membership in one step, and answers 201 with a session. The organization starts with the default budget (BUDGET_USD). Email addresses are normalized (trimmed, lowercased) before any lookup or storage, so Ana@Example.com and ana@example.com are the same account. Passwords are hashed with Argon2id (64 MiB, 3 iterations, 2 threads). A hash created with weaker parameters is re-hashed on the next successful login. When a rule fails, the response is 422 validation_failed with the details in error.fields. email · Trimmed and lowercased; max 254 characters; a plain address with a dot in the domain. password · 10 to 128 charac

With EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true, registration creates the account but opens no session: it answers 202 with verification_required and sends a one-time link (random token stored as a hash, valid for 24 hours). It needs AUTH_ENABLED=true, UI_BASE_URL and SMTP (SMTP_*) or EMAIL_DEV_LOG=true, which writes the links to the log instead of sending them. With TRIAL_ENABLED=true (which also needs AUTH_ENABLED=true), POST /api/v1/auth/trial creates a throwaway account with its own organization and returns, exactly once, the generated email, a password (format XXXX-XXXX-XXXX) and expires_at. Only the password hash is stored. GET /api/v1/auth/config tells the UI which features are on. POST /auth/login with

Login failures are counted per account. After five wrong passwords the account is locked for 15 minutes and further attempts answer 429 account_locked with a Retry-After header. An unknown email is checked against a dummy hash, so a missing account takes as long as a wrong password. On top of that there are per-email and per-IP limiters. Counters live in Redis when REDIS_URL is set (they survive restarts) and in memory otherwise. IP limits honour X-Forwarded-For only from addresses in TRUSTED_PROXIES. items.h: Sessions: access token and rotating refresh token
items.x: The access token is a short-lived (15 minutes) HS256 JWT carrying the user, the organization and the role, sent in Authorization: Bearer. The refresh token is an opaque random value, valid for 30 days, stored server-side only as a SHA-256 hash and delivered in the wfai_refresh cookie (HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Secure by default, Path=/api/v1/auth). It never appears in a JSON body. /auth/refresh and /auth/logout act on that cookie, so they require the X-WFAI-CSRF header and reject requests with Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site or with an Origin outside ALLOWED_ORIGINS (or the host itself). Each refresh rotates the token inside its family: Presenting an already-used refresh token revokes the whole

Each user can turn on a TOTP second factor: POST /auth/mfa/setup returns secret and otpauth_uri (for the QR code), and POST /auth/mfa/enable with a valid code turns it on and returns 8 recovery codes, shown exactly once. From then on, a login with the right password opens no session: it answers 200 with mfa_required and a 5-minute mfa_token, and the session opens with POST /auth/mfa/verify ({mfa_token, code}). A TOTP code cannot be replayed, and wrong codes count toward the same lockout as passwords. An organization can require two-factor authentication from its members (login returns mfa_enrollment_required with an enrolment token) or require SSO (a password login by anyone who is not an ow

Each membership has one role: owner, admin, member or viewer. A role is a set of permissions named resource:action, and each is a strict superset of the one below. The role is re-read from the database on every request, so demoting or removing a member takes effect immediately rather than when the token expires. GET /auth/me returns the role and its permissions list. An owner can assign any role; an admin can assign and manage only roles below admin and cannot change their own; nobody grants a role above their own. The last owner cannot be removed (409 last_owner). Agents never receive approval permissions such as artifacts:approve: their authority cannot approve what they themselves propose

A user can belong to several organizations, with a different role in each. GET /auth/me returns the user and the orgs list with names and roles. POST /auth/switch-org with {org_id} opens a new session in another of the user's organizations and revokes the previous refresh-token family; asking for an organization without membership answers 403 forbidden. All member management happens inside the actor's organization, and users from other organizations are reported as not found: GET /auth/members lists the members (members:read). POST /auth/members with {email, role} adds a user who already has an account (members:invite). PATCH /auth/members/{id} with {role} changes the role (members:manage).

Admins and owners invite an email address with a role they are allowed to assign (POST /api/v1/invitations). The server stores only the SHA-256 of the one-time token and returns the plaintext exactly once. It does not send email: the inviter shares the /invite?token=... link served by the frontend. A new invitation to the same address revokes the previous pending one, and links expire after 7 days. POST /api/v1/auth/invitations/accept is public and takes {token, name, password}. A new person picks a name and a password; an existing account proves ownership with its current password, under the same lockout as login. items.h: Tenant isolation with Postgres row-level security
items.x: Role checks decide what a user may do; row-level security decides which rows exist for them. Every tenant table has the tenant_isolation policy, which compares org_id with app_current_org(), and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applies it even to the table owner. Each request runs in a transaction that starts with set_config('app.org_id', ..., true): the setting is transaction-local, so a pooled connection cannot carry one tenant into another request. It fails closed: without app.org_id, no row is visible or writable. Every application connection runs SET ROLE app_user (DB_APP_ROLE), a role that is not a superuser, has no BYPASSRLS and owns no table. For that role the audit log is append-only (UPDAT

The auth router is mounted at /api/v1/auth and the invitation router at /api/v1/invitations. Permissions are checked by middleware before the handler runs, and the service re-reads the actor's current membership on every member operation. Errors use the shape {"error": {"code", "message"}}. The API reference lists the remaining routes and the security model covers the threat analysis. A skill is reusable know-how that an agent loads when it needs it: a folder with a SKILL.md file and optional text resources, in the open Agent Skills format. This page is for anyone who writes, imports or reviews skills. Since it is plain prompt text plus one gateway tool, it works the same with every model provider.

A package is a folder whose only required file is SKILL.md: a YAML frontmatter block followed by markdown instructions. It may include supporting files such as templates, examples, reference documents or scripts, always as text. Each version stores its files in the organization's Drive, at /Shared/Skills/<name>/v<n>/, and the database keeps the manifest: path, size and sha256 of each file. Versions are immutable; restoring an old version creates a new version with the same content.

SKILL.md must be valid UTF-8, start with a --- line and close the block with another one. The instructions after the frontmatter cannot be empty. The parser understands a small subset of YAML, on purpose: Scalars, quoted strings and > or | blocks. Inline or block lists. A single level of nested map, only for metadata. It rejects anchors, aliases, tags, inline maps and tabs in indentation. Other top-level scalar keys are preserved on import and export (up to 20 keys and 300 bytes per value), so a round trip loses nothing. The in-app editor does not show compatibility or those extra keys: saving from the editor drops them. name · Yes · Pattern ^[a-z0-9-]{1,64}$. Unique per organization and imm

These caps are validated on create, edit and import. A violation returns a stable error code, for example file_too_large, too_many_files, extension_not_allowed or zip_bomb. Each segment starts with a letter or digit and uses A-Z, a-z, 0-9, ., _ or -, up to 64 characters. The backend ships a catalog of starter skills embedded in the binary, in Spanish and English, in the same format as an import. There are 55 per language today, including bank-reconciliation, b2b-proposal, service-contract-review, month-end-close, client-email and project-plan. The first time an organization opens the library, they are created as active in its language. If the organization already has any skill, even a deleted one, none are created, and deleted starters do not come back. Role templates declare default_skills (names only) and agents of that role receive them without needing an assignment.

A skill is in one of four statuses: draft, in_review, active or disabled. Members (skills:write permission) create drafts, edit, import and restore versions. Administrators (skills:review permission) approve, reject, disable and delete. An import always enters in_review. If a member edits an active skill, the new version lands in in_review and agents keep using the approved one. If an administrator edits it, the edit counts as the review and it becomes active. A review names the version the reviewer read: if it is no longer current, it fails with stale_review. File hashes are checked again before activation. Every saved version is scanned and the warnings are stored for the reviewer. The scan informs; it does not decide: the reviewer sees everything before approving. injection: a file's injection score exceeds the threshold. script: the package ships executable files as text (py, js, sh). allowed_tools: the frontmatter declares allowed-tools. import_note: the import adjusted something, for example it skipped an empty file. Import a .zip or a single SKILL.md with POST /api/v1/skills/import (multipart field file). Validation is strict: it rejects absolute paths or paths with .., backslashes, drive letters, symlinks and special files, encrypted entries, duplicates that differ only in case, and zip

Every route lives under /api/v1, behind authentication and per-organization isolation. A review body carries the decision (approve or reject), the reviewed version and a note. POST /skills/{id}/versions/{n}/restore · skills:write · Creates a new version with the content of version n. POST /skills/{id}/submit · skills:write · Moves from draft to in_review. POST /skills/{id}/review · skills:review · Approves or rejects a specific v

An assignment links a skill to an agent through PUT and DELETE on /api/v1/agents/{id}/skills/{skillId}, with the agents:write permission. There are also role defaults: the names in a role template's default_skills reach every agent of that role without an explicit assignment. An agent only receives a skill if it is assigned (or is a default of its role), is neither deleted nor disabled, and has an approved version. While an edit waits for review, the approved version is served. In any other case the load is denied with skill_not_available.

Disclosure is progressive, in two steps. On every run, the backend adds to the request only the name and description of the skills the agent can use, with caps: at most 12 skills, 240 characters per description and 3000 bytes in total. The runtime renders them in the prompt with an explicit rule: a skill guides how to work and never grants tools, connections, permissions, autonomy or approvals. If a skill applies, the agent asks for it with a tool request. The Tool Gateway serves it as a native read tool, subject to the kill switch, pause and audit, and answers with the approved version's body without frontmatter plus the file list. With file it returns a single resource.

items.h: Limits and cleaning of loaded text
items.x: Once loaded, the skill enters the task context with several safeguards: The text travels in its own channel (loaded_skills) as trusted organization configuration, inside dedicated delimiters, because a person approved that exact version. It is still cleaned (invisible characters, credentials, forged delimiters) and scored for injection. It is bounded in the backend (24,000 characters per answer, 4 loads per task) and again in the runtime (3 skills, 12,000 characters each, 20,000 in total). Scripts are inert text: running them requires the code tool, with human approval.

This guide takes AI Workforce OS to your own Linux server with the repository's production compose file: Caddy terminates TLS and routes to the frontend (Next.js) and the backend (Go), which talks to the agent runtime (Python), Postgres and Redis. It covers installation, day-to-day operation (updates, migrations, backups) and the reduced layout of the public demo.

docker-compose.prod.yml is standalone: it is not combined with the development docker-compose.yml. It serves a single domain. Caddy sends /api/* and /ws to the backend (internal port 8080) and everything else to the frontend (internal port 3000). Only Caddy publishes ports: 80, 443 TCP and 443 UDP. Every other service lives on the internal network, declared with internal: true and therefore without internet access. The runtime also joins the egress network to call model provider APIs, and Caddy joins the edge network. The frontend uses relative paths (/api/v1) and derives the WebSocket URL from window.location (wss:// under HTTPS), so a single-domain deployment does not need any baked NEXT_P

A Linux server with Docker Engine and the Docker Compose v2 plugin, with ports 80 and 443 open in the firewall. A domain with a DNS A record (and AAAA if you have IPv6) pointing to the server. Let's Encrypt fails if DNS does not resolve yet. Access to the images on GHCR. If the packages are private, run docker login ghcr.io with a token that has read:packages. Alternative: build the images on the server itself with --build. A DeepSeek key: the production compose file requires DEEPSEEK_API_KEY. The Anthropic key is optional.

The examples use example.com as the domain and OWNER and TAG as placeholders. All state lives in named volumes, and .env.prod stays out of git: the repository .gitignore already ignores .env.*. Clone the repository on the server and copy the .env.prod.example template to .env.prod. Restrict its permissions with chmod 600 .env.prod. Fill in the variables. The block below shows a complete minimal .env.prod. The template ships filler values such as CAMBIAR_openssl_rand_hex_32. If you keep them, anyone who reads them in the repository can sign tokens or log into the database. Replace each one with your own random secret.

The backend reads the environment at startup and validates the combination before it opens its port: if something is inconsistent, the process exits with an error that names the variable. The runtime reads its variables when it uses them. The frontend reads nothing at runtime: its values are fixed at build time. A language model can be tricked: it processes untrusted text and it can act. That is why AI Workforce OS bounds damage with deterministic controls in the backend (Go), not with prompt instructions. This page is for anyone evaluating or operating the platform: it describes what is implemented and, at the end, what is not.

Agents only produce tool requests; the backend decides whether they run. The Tool Gateway checks every request in this order: Controls: kill switch, agent pause, read-only mode and tools or actions switched off. The connection grant for that agent. Validation: connection status, granted capability, the grant's maximum risk and usage limits. A scan for secrets in the outgoing arguments. Approval reasons: the policy engine collects every verdict and keeps the strictest (deny beats approval, and approval beats allow). The agent runtime never receives connection credentials. If an organization stores its own model key, that key does travel to the runtime on each call, because the runtime is what

Connection credentials (OAuth tokens, API keys) and each organization's own model keys are stored encrypted with AES-256-GCM in an envelope scheme. A key-encryption key (KEK) held outside the database wraps a versioned per-organization data key (DEK), and the DEK encrypts each secret with a random nonce. The additional authenticated data includes organization, record, version and kind, so a ciphertext copied to another row or organization does not decrypt. Without a KEK (CONNECTIONS_KEK, 32 bytes in base64) the vault fails closed: it neither stores nor reads live credentials. It can load several KEKs at once for rotation (CONNECTIONS_KEK_PREVIOUS), and each credential has active and retired

An agent can request an action, never approve it. People with the admin or owner role decide, and the role comes from the session token, not from the request body. Each approval is bound by hash to the exact arguments approved, is consumed once and is revalidated before execution, because rules may have changed while it waited. An approval for an interactive request expires after 30 minutes (APPROVAL_TIMEOUT), and an expiry counts as a rejection. Project approvals do not expire by default: the system sends an hourly reminder while they are pending. There is a floor no organization rule can weaken: declared high risk, actions on the mandatory-approval list (APPROVAL_ACTIONS) and agents at the

An action through an external connection passes three filters in series: the capability the provider declares, the grant the organization gives to a specific agent, and the policy and approval of the action itself. A grant can only narrow what the connection allows. The recommended pattern is to keep a read-only connection separate from a write one. Limits are computed from the usage table in Postgres, so they survive restarts. An agent cannot change its own autonomy, permissions or rules, and any deny rule beats an allow rule. Before every runtime call, the maximum estimated cost is reserved against the request, the agent, the department and the organization. Afterwards it is reconciled using the higher of the cost the runtime reports and the one the backend recomputes. When a request, agent or department cap is reached, the work pauses and a person decides whether to raise it; the organization cap makes the call fail. Structural limits also guard against loops: delegation depth (5), retries per task, time per task, plan and project size, and a per-organization queue (8 concurrent calls by default). The kill switch has two levels. Any admin or owner can activate it; lifting it requires the owner role and a written reason. It can also be imposed with the KILL_SWITCH environment variable (freeze or lockdown), which no API call can lift: the variable must be removed and the process reloaded. There are finer controls: pausing an agent (it denies the agent's new tool calls and new work), read-only mode for the organization or an agent (it keeps reading and proposing, but effects are denied) and switching off a tool or a single action, for example email or email.send. Held actions return to the approval queue and must be approved again: nothing runs by inertia when a control is lifted. none ·

The audit log is a per-organization hash chain: each entry includes the hash of the previous one (SHA-256 over a canonical representation with sequence, organization, timestamp, actor, action, entity and details). Changing, deleting, reordering or inserting an entry breaks the chain from that point, and truncating the tail is detected against the chain head. Before being chained, every entry goes through a scrubber that keeps metadata only: it replaces content fields (bodies, arguments, subjects, summaries) and credential-like keys with [redacted], masks embedded secrets and cuts strings to 300 characters. Audited events include authentication, policy decisions, approvals, tool executions, a

Tables holding organization data use row-level security (RLS) in Postgres. Each transaction sets the organization with a transaction-scoped set_config, the policies filter by it and the application connects with a role without BYPASSRLS. An integration test covers isolation between organizations. Access tokens last 15 minutes and refresh tokens 30 days. After 5 failed attempts the account is locked for 15 minutes. Sign-in also allows 10 attempts per 15 minutes per email and 20 per IP (in Redis when available, in memory otherwise). For nonexistent accounts a password hash is still computed, so response time does not reveal whether the user exists. There is single sign-on with OIDC (with PKCE)

items.h: Untrusted content and the code sandbox
items.x: Everything that comes from outside (emails, API responses, files) goes through a deterministic pipeline before reaching the model: text is normalized (NFKC, invisible characters removed), credentials, one-time codes and card numbers are masked, markdown images and links are neutralized, the text is cut (4,000 characters by default), scored with injection heuristics and wrapped as data in a delimited block. A high score flags the task and forces approval of its actions. The score is a signal, not a barrier: the barrier is permissions, approvals and limits. Code an agent wants to run is shown in full to a person, and the backend only sends it to the runner after approval. Changing the code or

There are no certifications (neither SOC 2 nor ISO) and the project is not ready for regulated enterprise environments. These are the known limits: Single sign-on is OIDC only: SAML is not implemented. Audit export is an unsigned JSONL or CSV dump, and nothing anchors the chain head off the server automatically. Recovery after a restart assumes a single instance: with several replicas, the per-organization queue, budget reservations and some counters are per process or last-writer-wins. A call already sent to the runtime finishes even if the kill switch is activated. There is no per-risk approval permission: deciding equals being admin or owner. Everything you need to get the most out of your office of AI employees, screen by screen. Start with “Getting started” and follow the order, or jump to what interests you.

AI Workforce OS is a 3D virtual office where the employees are AI agents. In about five minutes you will create your account, ask for your first task, decide an approval and read the report the team leaves behind.

Every new account creates its own organization, separate from everyone else's, and you become its Owner. The office starts with 1,000 welcome coins for the Shop. Open app.workforceai.es and press “Create a new account”. Enter “Your name”, “Your company name”, “E-mail” and a “Password” of at least 10 characters. Press “Create account”. If you receive a confirmation e-mail, open its link within 24 hours to enter your office. If you want to look around before signing up, press “Or try it without signing up” (when available) to get a trial username and password valid for 24 hours. A trial account's work is lost when it expires; create an account if you want to keep it.

When you sign in you land on the Office: a 3D scene with your team and, at the bottom, a bar to talk to the whole office the way you would talk to a team lead. Press one of the shortcuts above the bar: “Say hi”, “Finance”, “$50,000 proposal”, “Sales are down” or “Hire 2 people”. Or type your request in the bar “Write to the office: say hi, ask or request something…” and press “Send”. Read the answer in the office chat, right above the bar. If it is a task, you will see who it was assigned to and why. If the server has no model provider configured, the AI runs in simulation mode: answers are scripted, there is no model cost, and the flow is the same as with a real model. Start with “$50,000 p

Each person in the scene is an agent and moves according to what they are doing: working at their desk, meeting others to plan, or waiting in the approvals area. Check the “Live activity” box at the top left to follow every step the agents take. Look at the status in the office chat header: “In progress: planning”, “running” or “waiting for your approval”. Click an employee to open their panel, see their work and write to them directly. Drag to rotate the view, use the scroll wheel to zoom and hold the right button to pan.

When an agent wants to do something sensitive, it stops and waits for your decision. Nothing continues until you decide. Open the pending approvals tray at the bottom left of the office. Read what the agent wants to do and its risk level. Press “Approve” to let it continue or “Reject” to stop it. Deciding approvals requires the Admin or Owner role. If your role cannot, the card tells you so and shows no buttons. Rejecting is a valid answer too: that is what the human step is for.

The office is a 3D scene and you choose the point of view. While no employee is selected, the bottom right corner reminds you of the mouse gestures. A request in the office bar is enough for a single task. When the work has many parts, use a project: it brings together objectives, tasks split among your employees, approvals and budget. Here you learn to create it, launch it and follow it to the end.

items.h: Decide whether you need a project
items.x: A project is a plan with several objectives. Each objective splits into tasks done by an agent, and some are human steps, such as an approval or a milestone only you can sign off. It suits you when: The work has many parts or several phases. Several agents need to move forward in parallel. You want to set a budget before starting. You will repeat the same work and a template helps. For something small, ask for it directly in the office bar.

Open “Projects” in the side menu and press “New project”. Write the “Project goal” in your own words, or pick a template in “Template”. With “No template (free plan)”, the plan is built from your goal. If you picked a template, fill in its parameters and check the “Plan preview”: tasks, human gates, longest chain, parallel work and estimated cost. Enter a “Budget (USD, optional)” or leave it empty to have one suggested from the estimate. Press “Create draft”. Creating the draft spends no budget: the project has not started yet.

items.h: Review the plan and launch it
items.x: The draft shows the “Project plan”: each objective with its tasks and the assigned agent. Until you launch it, you can adjust it. Change a task's title or the agent doing it, and add acceptance criteria, one per line. Check the “Estimate”: “Likely cost (P50)”, “Pessimistic cost (P90)” and the estimated duration. In “Quality review”, choose “Do not review”, “Only when the agent is unsure” or “Always”. Make sure “Validation” says the plan is valid. Enter the “Approved budget (USD)”. The app suggests P90 plus 10%. Press “Launch project”. Only tasks with acceptance criteria are reviewed, and each review counts toward the budget. If the budget is below the likely cost, the project may pause for l

items.h: Provide the data the project needs
items.x: Some projects need data to compute real figures. In that case the draft shows the “Before you start” card, and what you provide is stored in the project's Inputs folder, where all its agents read it. Press “Upload file” to upload the data from your computer. Or press “Pick from the drive” to use files already in Files. If you only want to try it, press “Use sample data”: fictional data that fills in what is missing. If you do not have the data, press “Launch without this data”: it is recorded and the agents will work with explicit assumptions.

items.h: Follow progress and control the project
items.x: Each card in the Projects list shows the status, a bar with finished steps over the total, tasks “to approve”, those with problems and spending against the budget. Inside the project you see the same bar at the top. Depending on its status, the project offers “Pause”, “Resume” or “Cancel”. Cancel asks for confirmation and stops any unfinished tasks.

The tabs follow a working order: Health tells you if there is a problem, Map shows where, Kanban and lanes are for acting, and Timeline is for replanning. Health · Knowing whether something is wrong Map · Seeing where in the plan the problem is Timeline · Replanning dates and dependencies Kanban · Acting on tasks by status Agent lanes · Acting on each agent's tasks Delegation · Seeing who asked whom for work Approvals · Deciding what you must authorize and revoking remembered decisions Plan changes · Reviewing proposed changes to the plan Costs · Seeing what has been spent

items.h: Start from a template or save your own
items.x: In “Projects”, press “Use template” on one of the listed templates, or “See all” to open the library. In the library, search by name or description and press “Use”, “Duplicate” to adapt it, or “New template” to build one from scratch. To repeat a project you already ran, open it and press “Save as template”. Saving as a template keeps the project's structure; results and costs are not copied.

items.h: Collect the bonus when it finishes
items.x: When a project finishes successfully with at least two tasks done, your organization receives a one-time coin bonus. With the default settings it is 20 coins plus 2 per finished task, capped at 100. A cancelled or failed project does not receive it. Coins are only earned by finished work, cannot be bought with money and are spent on cosmetic items in the Shop.

items.t: Chats and Files: pick up conversations and find what was produced
items.x: Chats keeps what you have discussed with your agents and with the people in your organization. Files gathers the documents your agents create and the ones you upload, with versions and a trash so nothing gets lost. Here you learn to find, write, upload and recover.

items.t: Chats and Files: pick up conversations and find what was produced
items.x: In Chats, the “Conversations” list starts with “General”, which shows everything in order: what you wrote to the office and what you wrote to each agent. Below it there is one thread per agent. Open “Chats” in the side menu. Press “General” to see everything, or an agent to see only their thread. Agents with recent activity come first and a number shows unread messages. To search, type in “Search titles and messages…”. The list is replaced by the “Results”, with the match highlighted. Press “Clear search” to go back to the list.

items.t: Chats and Files: pick up conversations and find what was produced
items.h: Write to the office or to an agent
items.x: Pick “General” or an agent in the list. Type your message in the box at the bottom and send it. Check under your message which agents it was sent to: in General, the office routes it to the right agent; in an agent's thread, it goes straight to them. In an agent's thread, “See in the office” takes you to their desk in the 3D scene.

items.t: Chats and Files: pick up conversations and find what was produced
items.h: Talk to the people on your team
items.x: The “Team” section of the list gathers chats between people: the organization-wide channel, direct messages and groups, which you can also add agents to. Press “New” in the “Team” section. Choose “Direct message” and a person, or “Group”, a name and its members (people and agents). Press “Create” and write. Use @ to mention people or agents. Admins can also create “Department” and “Project” channels. With the Read only role you can read chats but not write.

items.t: Chats and Files: pick up conversations and find what was produced
items.x: Every time you ask the office for work, the agents' internal conversation about it is kept in “Past conversations”. It is read only: to keep talking, write in General or to an agent. The messages that started a piece of work carry “View report” and “View project” to jump straight to the result. Click a conversation in “Past conversations” to read it. Use “Rename” to give it a title you recognize. Press “Archive” to take it out of the list; “Show archived” shows them and “Restore” brings them back. Press “Delete” and confirm with “Yes, delete” to erase it with its messages. Deleting a conversation erases it for good along with its messages. Only an Admin or the Owner can do it.

items.t: Chats and Files: pick up conversations and find what was produced
items.x: Files holds the documents your agents create and the ones you upload. You start at “Home”, with four root folders: Open “Files” in the side menu. Press a folder to enter it. The table shows “Name”, “Last change”, “Version”, “Size” and “Updated”. Press a file to open it in the right panel. Text, CSV, Markdown, JSON and YAML files are previewed there; anything else opens with “Download”. Use the folder path at the top to go back: press a segment to go up to that folder, or “Home” to return to the root. The “Last change” column tells you whether an agent, a person or the system made it. Agent desks · One folder per agent with its work · Each agent, its own Projects · One folder per project, wit

items.t: Chats and Files: pick up conversations and find what was produced
items.x: Enter a folder: you cannot upload at “Home”. Press “Upload” and choose one or more files, or drag them from your computer onto the screen. Drop the files when you see the notice with the destination folder and wait for them to finish uploading. By default, each file can be up to 25 MB. Which agents can read it depends on the folder, as the table above shows.

items.t: Chats and Files: pick up conversations and find what was produced
items.h: Search by name, content or meaning
items.x: Type in “Search files…” and press Enter. The search looks at names and the text inside files, and each result shows a snippet. Press a result to go to its folder, or “Close” to return to the list. Turn on “By meaning” to search passages by what they mean, also inside PDFs and long documents. Each result shows the page and the snippet. If search by meaning is not available, the app tells you and shows results by words.

items.t: Chats and Files: pick up conversations and find what was produced
items.h: Recover an earlier version or a deleted file
items.x: Every time a person or an agent changes a file, a version is saved, and “Move to trash” only sends it to the “Trash”, where you can restore it. Open a file and look at its “Version history”. Press a version (v1, v2…) to see how it was. Press “Restore” if you prefer that version. A new version is created with that content; history is never erased. To recover a deleted file, press “Trash” and then “Restore” next to the file. It goes back to its folder. Press “Trash” again to return to your files. Moving a file to the trash requires the Admin or Owner role.

items.t: Approvals and security: you stay in control
items.x: Your AI employees prepare and propose, but sensitive decisions are yours. Here you learn to decide approvals, review costs before running, set limits and permissions, and stop all activity with one click.

items.t: Approvals and security: you stay in control
items.h: Understand when an employee asks for permission
items.x: When an agent wants to do something that needs your sign-off, it stops and waits in the office's approvals area. Each notice says who is asking, which action it is, the details and the risk level (low, medium or high). An agent can ask for approval, but never grant it. How much each employee asks depends on its autonomy level, which you see in its panel and in “What each employee can do”: Sending an email, creating a calendar event, posting to Slack or LinkedIn, and creating GitHub issues or comments always ask for approval, whatever the level. Suggest only · It does not run them: they are recorded as a suggestion and a person carries them out Approve each action · Each one waits for your ap

items.t: Approvals and security: you stay in control
items.x: Open the pending approvals tray at the bottom left of the office. It opens by itself when a new one arrives, and you can hide or show it. Read the card's title, details and risk. Press “Approve” to let the agent continue or “Reject” to stop that action. Deciding requires the Admin or Owner role. If your role can only see the approval, the card tells you so and shows no buttons. You can also decide from the “Approvals” section of the Dashboard.

items.t: Approvals and security: you stay in control
items.x: Open app.workforceai.es/approvals in your phone's browser and sign in. Press “Enable notifications” to hear when something is waiting for your decision. Open the approval and decide with “Approve” or “Reject”. The notification only shows the title and risk; the decision is always made inside the app, signed in. On iPhone, add the app to your Home Screen first. If an approval needs two different people, the card shows how many approvals it has.

items.t: Approvals and security: you stay in control
items.x: For internal project actions that can be undone, the card offers to remember your decision. External actions never qualify: sending, publishing, paying, deleting and running code always ask. Tick “Remember this decision for this kind of action”. Choose for how long: “This session (about 8 hours)” or “This project”. If you chose the project, tick “Also for the other agents of this project” to extend it. Press “Approve for this session” or “Approve for this project”. Revoke a remembered decision at any time from the project's “Approvals” tab.

items.t: Approvals and security: you stay in control
items.x: Before running a request that may touch connections with write access, the office asks you to review its plan on the Security screen, under “Plan review”. Open “Settings” and go to “Security”. In “Plan review”, read the estimated cost (with its likely maximum), the approximate time, the “Connections it could touch” and the approvals expected. Take out any tasks you do not want with “Remove”. Press “Approve and run” or “Reject”. It is an estimate, not an invoice. If a request's maximum estimated cost goes over the confirmation threshold, the office also waits for your confirmation before starting.

items.t: Approvals and security: you stay in control
items.x: For a per-employee cap, open the Dashboard, go to “Costs & errors” and enter its “Monthly cap (USD)” under “Budget limits”. Press “Save”; leaving it empty removes the cap. To see every limit, open “Settings”, go to “Security” and scroll to “Spend limits”: each row shows the scope, period, usage, limit and what happens “When reached” (“Warn”, “Pause and ask” or “Block”). To limit a connection, open “Connections”, go to the “Limits” tab, set “Uses per day”, “Writes per day” and “Monthly budget (USD)”, and press “Save limits”. An employee that hits its cap shows as “Paused” under “Budget limits”.

items.t: Approvals and security: you stay in control
items.h: Decide what each employee can do
items.x: Connecting an account is not granting access: each permission is assigned separately, following least privilege. Integrations with real accounts are still being tested. Open “Settings”, go to “Connections” and press “Connect”. Follow the “Connect an account” wizard: “Connection name”, “Connection type”, “What will it be able to do?” and, if you like, “Assign to employees (optional)”. Open the “Permissions by employee” tab and click a cell (employee and connection) to view or change its permissions. Grant write permissions from that same tab. If there is more than one admin, another person must approve the grant. Check “What each employee can do” and the “Usage log” to see what happened.

items.t: Approvals and security: you stay in control
items.x: Your connections' keys and secrets are sent once and stored encrypted on the server. The screen never shows them again: to change one, you rotate it. The AI model does not see them either, because tools are run by the server, not the model. With a real model, task text does travel to the configured model provider, so check its terms before using sensitive data. AI Workforce OS does not hold any security certifications today.

items.t: Approvals and security: you stay in control
items.x: The “Security and control” screen (Settings, Security) gathers the office's brakes. Nothing you do here deletes data. Alerts can freeze the office automatically, but that option is off by default. Global read-only mode · Employees keep reading and proposing, but send and change nothing Pause employees · A paused employee starts no new tasks and uses no connections, and resumes where it left off Stop by tool · Switches a tool off for everyone; any admin stops it and only the Owner turns it back on Operating hours · Outside hours, new work waits in plain sight; work already running is not interrupted Unusual activity alerts · Warn about a spend spike, bursts of tool requests, many rejected app

items.t: Approvals and security: you stay in control
items.x: “Stop everything” is in Settings and in the Security center. Any admin can stop, but only the Owner can lift the lock. Nothing is deleted. There are two levels: Press “Stop everything” and choose the level. Write a reason if you like and confirm with “Yes, stop everything”. To resume, the Owner opens “Security”, writes the “Reason to resume” and presses “Lift lock”. When you resume, actions that were on hold ask for approval again. Everything stopped · Nothing new starts and connection use is blocked; accounts stay connected Full lockdown · Also suspends all connections and cancels pending sends

items.t: Skills: reusable know-how for your agents
items.x: A skill is a written guide an agent looks up while it works, for example how to reconcile a bank statement or write a weekly report. Here you learn to find skills, write or import your own, approve them and give them to an agent.

items.t: Skills: reusable know-how for your agents
items.x: Each skill has a name, a description of when to use it and step-by-step instructions. It can include resource files, input and output examples and quality criteria. On every task, the agent only sees the name and description of its skills. It receives the full text only if it asks for it. A skill only brings knowledge: it never grants tools, connections or permissions. The agent's role and your organization still decide that, and sensitive actions still ask for your approval.

items.t: Skills: reusable know-how for your agents
items.x: The library starts with 55 built-in skills, already active and written in Spanish or English. They carry the “Built-in” label and cover sales, finance, legal, human resources, support, product, data and engineering. For example: Bank reconciliation and month-end close. Lead qualification and sales call prep. NDA review and service contract review. Job descriptions and interview questions. Support replies and complaint handling. Product requirements, SQL query explanations and a code review checklist. Your agents' roles already include some; on the skill they show as “From role”.

items.t: Skills: reusable know-how for your agents
items.x: Open “Skills” in the side menu. Type a topic in “Search skills…”, for example “report” or “sales”. The list filters instantly. Filter by status with “All”, “Active”, “In review”, “Drafts” or “Disabled”; each filter shows how many there are. Click a card to open it and see its status, its source (“Built-in”, “Created”, “Imported” or “From a task”), its version and how many agents have it. Skills in review open directly on the “Review” tab.

items.t: Skills: reusable know-how for your agents
items.h: Read a skill before using it
items.x: Each skill has four tabs: The scan warns, for example, about a “Possible instruction injection” or that the skill “Contains a script”. Scripts are stored as text and never run on their own: running one needs code.run with human approval. You can take any skill with you using “Download .zip” or “Download SKILL.md”. Content · The description, the instructions and the resource files Review · Everything an agent would receive, with the “Scan warnings” Versions · Every saved version, with a “Restore” option Agents · Who has it and whether it arrives “Assigned” or “From role”

items.t: Skills: reusable know-how for your agents
items.x: You can write it from scratch or start from work already done: in the “Tasks” tab of an agent's panel, a finished task offers “Save as skill”, which pre-fills the draft. Press “New skill”. Write the “Name” in lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, for example bank-reconciliation. It cannot be changed later. Fill in “Description: when to use it”. It is the only thing the agent sees on every task, so say what it does and when it fits. Write the “Instructions” in Markdown and, if you like, add “Resource files”, “Examples” and “Quality criteria”. Press “Create draft” and then, from its page, “Send for review”. Resource files must be text (md, txt, csv, json, yaml, py, js or sh), up to 512 KB eac

items.t: Skills: reusable know-how for your agents
items.h: Import a skill you already have
items.x: Press “Import” and choose a .zip or .md file with a skill in SKILL.md format. If one with that name already exists, type another and press “Import with this name”. Read the whole skill on the “Review” tab, where it opens when done: it stays “In review” until someone approves it. A .zip must have SKILL.md at its root and weigh 4 MB at most.

items.t: Skills: reusable know-how for your agents
items.h: Activate it and assign it to an agent
items.x: Only what a person approved reaches an agent: a draft or a skill in review is given to no one. This is what each role can do: As an admin, open the “Review” tab, read the content and the warnings and press “Approve and activate”. “Reject” sends it back to draft with your note. Open the active skill and go to the “Agents” tab. Pick an agent in “Choose an agent…” and press “Assign”. To take it away, press “Remove” next to the agent. If you edit an active skill, agents keep using the approved version until the new one is approved. Read and download skills · Every role Create, import and send for review · Member, Admin and Owner Approve, disable or delete · Admin and Owner Assign to an agent or

items.t: Coins and the Shop: decorate your office with what your team earns
items.x: Every time your team of agents finishes work, your organization earns coins. In the Shop you trade them for items for your agents and your office. Here you learn how coins are earned, how to buy and how to use what you buy.

items.t: Coins and the Shop: decorate your office with what your team earns
items.x: Coins are only earned by finished work: they cannot be bought with money and there is no way to pay for more. Every new organization starts with 1,000 welcome coins, and after that the balance grows in three ways: When an agent finishes a task. When a project finishes successfully. When you reach the daily goal. Your balance shows at the top of the Shop, next to your total earned and spent.

items.t: Coins and the Shop: decorate your office with what your team earns
items.x: With the default settings, each task pays according to its size. A task with no size counts as M. If a quality review approves the result on the first try, the task pays 50% extra. If the review asked for rework, the task pays half its value. A project that finishes successfully with at least 2 tasks done pays a one-time bonus of 20 coins plus 2 per finished task, capped at 100. Failed, skipped, cancelled or blocked tasks, tasks with a rejected approval, and milestones or human steps pay nothing. Whoever runs the server can change these values. S · 5 M · 10 L · 20 XL · 40

items.t: Coins and the Shop: decorate your office with what your team earns
items.x: In the top bar you will see a daily goal, for example “Finish 1 task today” or “Get 1 task approved on the first try”, with its progress and reward. The goal changes every day and is the same for everyone. It only counts work already paid by the normal rules, and each day pays once at most. When you reach it, the chip shows “Done today”. The goal shows on medium or large screens, and does not appear if the coin system is turned off.

items.t: Coins and the Shop: decorate your office with what your team earns
items.x: The Shop has close to a thousand items, always sorted from cheapest to most expensive. Open “Shop” in the side menu. Pick a group: “Characters”, for your agents' clothes and accessories, or “Office”, for furniture and decor. Press a category. Characters has Outfits, Hats, Glasses, Headphones, Neckwear, Badges and Companions. Office has Desks, Chairs, Tables, Sofas, Cabinets, Dividers, Whiteboards, Equipment, Lights, Plants, Lamps, Rugs, Coffee machine, Posters, Bookshelves, Aquariums, Arcade, Trophies and Views. Press “All” to see the whole group, and “Show more” if the list is long. When you switch groups, the category goes back to “All”.

items.t: Coins and the Shop: decorate your office with what your team earns
items.x: Each card shows a preview, the rarity (Common, Rare or Epic), a description and the price. Check your coin balance at the top of the Shop. Press “Buy” on the item you want. If you cannot afford it, the button is disabled and the card says how many coins you are missing. Press “Equip from inventory” to use it: the purchase goes to your inventory and is not applied on its own. Buying, equipping and placing require the Member role or above. With Read only you can browse the Shop but not spend.

items.t: Coins and the Shop: decorate your office with what your team earns
items.x: Everything you buy lives in the “Inventory” tab. The action on each card depends on the kind of item: On the card, “Worn by” tells you which agents wear an item and “Placed in the office” that it is already in place. Character clothes and accessories · Pick the agent in “Character” and press “Equip”; “Take off” removes it Plants, lamps, rugs, coffee machine, posters, bookshelves, aquariums, arcade, trophies and views · Press “Place” to put it in its spot in the office and “Remove” to take it away Tables, sofas, cabinets, dividers, whiteboards, equipment and lights · Press “Place in the office”: the editor opens so you can put it wherever you like Desks and chairs · Press “Place in the office

items.t: Coins and the Shop: decorate your office with what your team earns
items.x: The “History” tab lists every movement with “When”, “What”, “Agent”, “Coins” and “Balance”, and below it an “Earned by agent” summary. Each line gives its reason: welcome coins, task finished, task approved on the first try, task finished after rework, project finished, daily goal reached or a purchase.

items.t: Coins and the Shop: decorate your office with what your team earns
items.x: Nothing about the work. Items are cosmetic only: a hat or a lamp changes how the office looks, but not what an agent can do, its permissions or the quality of its work. Think of coins as recognition for finished work.

items.t: Settings: configure your office in one place
items.x: Settings brings together your office's configuration, its security and your account on one screen. Here you learn what each card does and how to use the ones you will need most.

items.t: Settings: configure your office in one place
items.x: Open “Settings” at the bottom of the side menu. You will see cards grouped into Workspace, Safety and Account; some appear dimmed if your role cannot use them. Press a card to open its page. At the top you will see a path like “Settings > Office settings”. To go back, use the arrow in the path or your browser's Back button. The “?” button in the top bar opens a guided tour of this screen. Office settings · Workspace · Language, labels, motion and each employee's look Hire from template · Workspace · Adding an AI employee from a role template Templates · Workspace · Ready-made workflows to put to work Connections · Workspace · Email, calendar and other tools your team can use Set up your offi

items.t: Settings: configure your office in one place
items.x: Open “Office settings”. In “Language”, choose Español, English or Português for the interface. In “Labels”, turn “Show names” and “Activity bubbles” on or off, and adjust the “Label size”. Turn on “Reduce animations” if you prefer less motion. In “Employees”, change each one's name, nickname, job title, color, skin tone, hairstyle or accessory.

items.t: Settings: configure your office in one place
items.x: “Hire from template” adds an AI employee from a role template. The new agent starts with minimal autonomy and can never approve on its own. Only admins can use it. Open “Hire from template”. Pick a profession from the list. Type a name for the new agent, or leave it empty since it is optional. Press “Hire”. If the office is full or an agent with that name already exists, the app tells you and does not hire.

items.t: Settings: configure your office in one place
items.h: Put a ready-made flow to work
items.x: “Templates” opens the “Workflow template gallery”: flows with dependencies and parallel steps that your team runs while you approve what matters. Open “Templates”. Filter by category, for example “Sales” or “Finance”, or leave “All”. Review the steps of the template you are interested in and press “Use template”. Fill in the required details and press “Start flow”. Follow the progress in the office.

items.t: Settings: configure your office in one place
items.h: Describe your company and choose the AI model
items.x: If your workspace supports it, you will see the “Set up your office” card until you complete it, and “Team settings” afterwards. Open “Set up your office” and go through its steps: “Business type”, “Language and tone” and “Daily briefing”. Press “Finish”. Later, in “Team settings”, change the “Regional tone” of the office or of each agent and schedule the “Daily briefing”. In “AI model”, use the included model or press “Use my own key” to connect your OpenAI, Claude, Kimi, DeepSeek or other compatible account. Paste your “API key”, press “Test connection” and then “Save”. If the server has no model configured, the AI runs in simulation mode, with scripted answers. Your key is stored encrypte

items.t: Settings: configure your office in one place
items.x: “Connections” is where you link email, calendar and other tools so agents can work with your data. Connecting is not granting: permissions are assigned per employee. “Security” gathers permissions, spend limits, plan review, operating hours and the office's brakes. “Stop everything” immediately stops all external activity by every agent: only an admin can turn it on and, if it is already on, the card shows the level and takes you to Security. The step-by-step for permissions, limits and brakes is in the approvals and security guide.

items.t: Settings: configure your office in one place
items.x: Open “Account security” and press “Turn on” under “Two-step verification”. Scan the QR code with your authenticator app, enter the code it shows and press “Confirm and turn on”. Keep the recovery codes somewhere safe and press “I've saved them”. If you lost a device, press “Sign out everywhere”. Admins can set up single sign-on with Okta, Entra ID or Google, verify domains, require MFA and provision users with SCIM from “Single sign-on and identity”. Recovery codes are not shown again: without them and without your phone you will not be able to sign in.

items.t: Settings: configure your office in one place
items.h: Export your data or delete the organization
items.x: Open “Data & privacy”. Press “Export my organization's data” to download a ZIP with all your data and the drive's files. It never contains secrets, and you can generate one export per hour. To close the account, press “Delete my organization”, type the organization's name and your password, and confirm. If you change your mind, press “Cancel the deletion” before the period ends. Exporting is available to the Owner and admins; deleting, only to the Owner. The organization is permanently deleted 7 days after you confirm, with its agents, conversations, projects, files, connections and members, and no copy is kept. Export anything you want to keep first.

items.t: Settings: configure your office in one place
items.x: In the Account group you see the name, email and role you signed in with. Agents can never approve, whatever the role. These are the roles for people: Open “Members and invitations”. In “Invite someone”, enter the email, choose the role and press “Create invitation”. Copy the link and share it with the person: it is shown only once and expires in 7 days. Change a member's role, remove them or revoke a pending invitation from the same screen. An admin can only invite and manage Members and Read only users; the Owner can assign any role. Read only · See the office, chats, files, skills and the Shop, without changing anything Member · All of the above, plus ask for work, write in chats, upload

What a security or procurement team reviews before trusting us with data: which controls exist, how we handle data, which providers are involved and how to report a vulnerability. We describe what exists today, gaps included.

These are the security controls that exist today, as they can be checked in the code and in the deployment configuration. At the end there is a table of what we do not have yet. We hold no certifications (neither SOC 2 nor ISO 27001) and we do not claim compliance with any framework.

We only describe what exists. When a control depends on the operator's configuration, we say so. The design assumes that a language model can be fooled by untrusted text, so damage is limited with deterministic controls in the backend (Go) and not with instructions in the prompt: we do not promise that the model is never influenced, only that it can do nothing the backend does not authorize. The current public deployment runs on a single shared server. According to its configuration in the repository, the agent runtime is in simulation mode (it sends nothing to model providers) and the vault has no encryption key configured, so it stores no real credentials. More technical detail in the docu

Tables holding an organization's data use Postgres row-level security with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. Each request runs in a transaction that sets the organization with a local setting (app.org_id) and the policies filter on it. If it is not set, no row is visible or writable. The server works with a role (app_user) that is not a superuser, has no BYPASSRLS and owns no tables. Integration tests check isolation between two organizations. This is logical isolation inside one database, not an instance per customer.

Passwords hashed with Argon2id (64 MiB, 3 iterations, 2 threads), rehashed at the next sign-in if they were created with weaker parameters. 10 to 128 characters and at least two character classes. The account's own e-mail address and a short list of common passwords are rejected. After 5 failed attempts (password or verification code) the account is locked for 15 minutes. There are also rate limits per e-mail, per IP and per user on sign-in, sign-up, two-step verification, password recovery and SSO. For non-existent accounts an equivalent hash is computed, so response time does not reveal whether an e-mail exists. The access token is a 15-minute JWT. The refresh token is opaque, lasts 30 day

items.x: Single sign-on with any OpenID Connect provider (Okta, Entra ID, Google Workspace…): code flow with PKCE, state and nonce, and tokens signed only with RS256 or ES256. The client secret is stored encrypted in the vault. Domains verified with a DNS TXT record, re-checked every 24 hours. SSO and domain-based account creation only work with verified domains. Two-step verification with an authenticator app (TOTP) and 8 recovery codes. An organization can require it of all its members: anyone without it must enroll before getting a session. An organization can enforce SSO and turn off password sign-in. Owners keep their password as emergency access. SCIM 2.0 provisioning (users and groups) with on

Each membership has one of four roles: owner, admin, member or viewer, each a strict superset of the one below. Permissions have the form resource:action and are checked on the server before each operation. The role is read from the database on every request, so demoting or removing a member takes effect immediately. An admin can only assign the member and viewer roles and cannot change their own role, and the last owner cannot be removed or demoted. A person can belong to several organizations with a different role in each. There are no custom roles.

OAuth tokens, integration API keys and an organization's own AI keys are encrypted with AES-256-GCM in an envelope scheme: a key-encryption key (KEK) that lives outside the database wraps a per-organization data key, and that key encrypts each secret with a random nonce. The authenticated data binds each ciphertext to its organization and purpose, so if it is copied to another row or organization it does not decrypt. Without CONNECTIONS_KEK the vault fails closed: it neither stores nor reads real secrets. The KEK is rotated with CONNECTIONS_KEK_PREVIOUS and data keys can be rotated too. Revoking an OAuth connection suspends it, calls the provider's revocation endpoint and destroys the cipher

An agent can request an action but can never approve it. People with the admin or owner role decide. Each approval is bound by hash to the exact arguments, is consumed once and is re-validated before execution. It expires after 30 minutes by default (APPROVAL_TIMEOUT) and expiring counts as a rejection; project approvals do not expire by default and send hourly reminders. There are four autonomy levels per agent (suggest, approve_each, rules, autonomous). Integration actions with external, irreversible effects always ask for approval, and an approved e-mail waits at least 60 seconds before going out, during which it can still be cancelled. Before each runtime call the maximum estimated cost is reserved against the request, the agent and the organization, and afterwards it is reconciled with the larger of the cost reported by the runtime and the cost recomputed by the backend. When a cap is reached, work pauses until a person decides. Each call also carries its own cost cap, and there are limits on delegation depth, retries, time per call and parallel calls per organization. Operating hours prevent starting new work outside open hours. Anomaly detection applies four explainable rules (spend spike, burst of tool requests, serial rejected approvals and new recipient domains) and records each finding; it does not block on its own

The audit log is a hash chain per organization: each entry includes the SHA-256 of the previous one, so modifying, deleting, reordering or inserting an entry breaks the chain. For the application role it is append-only (UPDATE and DELETE revoked, plus triggers). Before being chained, each entry goes through a scrubber that replaces content and credential-looking keys with [redacted] and truncates long texts. Audited events include approvals, tool executions and denials, policy decisions, control changes, identity changes (SSO, MFA, password recovery, invitations) and exports and deletions. items.h: Data to AI models and untrusted content
items.x: Before text reaches the model, credentials and card numbers are masked, and the backend also masks one-time codes. External content (e-mails, API responses, files, web pages) is normalized, its markdown images and links are neutralized and it is wrapped in a block delimited as data. A heuristic injection score flags the task and adds approval reasons to actions with effects; it is a signal, not the barrier. The barrier is permissions, approvals and limits.
